plainTitle: The dateFormat setting in the config file is ignored

tldr.problem: A custom dateFormat in the config file has no effect.
tldr.cause: Config keys are lowercased, so dateFormat never overrides the default.
tldr.change: How keys are normalised in src/config.js.

counts.label: of 3 test cases fail
counts.explain: the test runs one case per fixture file (default, us, eu); only the two non-default formats fail

notes.text: This example is fictional. It shows what a crumbs page looks like.
Run the tests in a throwaway folder; they write fixture files (AGENTS.md).

steps.title: What the user sees
steps.simple: You set dateFormat in your config file, but the tool still prints the default format.
steps.detailed: With {"dateFormat": "DD.MM.YYYY"} in .tinydaterc.json, the CLI still prints dates as YYYY-MM-DD. The setting is read, but never used.
steps.deep: The file is found and parsed, so this is not a file-path problem. The value is lost between parsing the file and building the final options object.

steps.title: Only one small file is involved
steps.simple: The bug lives in the config loader, between reading the file and returning the options.
steps.detailed: The trail runs from the CLI entry point through loadConfig() and normalize() in src/config.js. formatDate() works correctly; it just receives the default pattern.
steps.deep: Starting from the symptom and following the value through the code is faster than reading the repo top-down. Once you see where the value disappears, the code after that point matters less.

steps.title: The CLI asks for the options
steps.simple: The command loads the config, then formats today's date with options.dateFormat.
steps.detailed: main() calls loadConfig() and passes options.dateFormat to formatDate(). Whatever loadConfig() returns under that exact key is what gets used.
steps.deep: The CLI reads options with plain property access, so it has no fallback for other spellings of the key. Any fix has to make sure this exact camelCase name ends up in the returned object.

steps.title: Keys are lowercased
steps.simple: Before merging, every key from the file is turned into lowercase letters.
steps.detailed: normalize() rewrites each key with toLowerCase(), so the user's dateFormat becomes dateformat.
steps.deep: The comment says this exists so users can write keys in any case. That intent is reasonable; the problem is that the defaults were never normalised the same way.

steps.title: Two different keys end up side by side
steps.simple: The default dateFormat and the user's dateformat both survive, and the code reads the default one.
steps.detailed: The spread merges DEFAULTS (camelCase) with the normalised keys (lowercase). They don't collide, so the user's value sits under a key nobody reads.

code.pointer: dateFormat (default) and dateformat (user) both end up in the result.

steps.deep: Object spread copies keys exactly as written, and JavaScript keys are case-sensitive. No error is raised, so the bug is silent: the user's value is present in the object, just under a name the CLI never reads.

steps.title: A case mismatch between defaults and user keys
steps.simple: The defaults use camelCase but user keys are lowercased, so they never match.
steps.detailed: normalize() is applied to user keys but not to DEFAULTS, and the rest of the code reads camelCase keys. Any multi-word setting is silently ignored, not only dateFormat.
steps.deep: timezone is unaffected only because it is a single lowercase word. This suggests the bug appears for every camelCase option, which is worth mentioning on the issue.

steps.title: Make keys match without losing case-insensitivity
steps.simple: Change how keys are normalised so user keys map back to the names the code reads.
steps.detailed: Map each user key, case-insensitively, onto the matching key in DEFAULTS. Keep accepting keys in any case, and add test cases for camelCase and lowercase input.
steps.deep: Watch for two keys that differ only in case, such as dateFormat and dateformat both set in one file. Decide which wins and test it, so the fix doesn't swap one silent bug for another.

why.simple: User keys are lowercased but defaults are not, so they never match.
why.detailed: normalize() lowercases user keys while DEFAULTS and the CLI use camelCase. The merged object holds both, and the CLI reads the default.
why.deep: Any multi-word option will be ignored the same way. Single-word options like timezone happen to work, which is why this went unnoticed.

questions: Should config keys stay case-insensitive, or is it fine to require exact camelCase names?
Are there other camelCase options planned that this should cover?

ignore.why: It looks involved because it prints the date, but it formats correctly with whatever pattern it gets.

glossary.camelCase: Writing multi-word names with a capital letter for each new word, like dateFormat.
glossary.normalise: Rewriting values into one consistent form, here lowercase key names.
glossary.DEFAULTS: The settings the tool uses when you don't set your own.
glossary.fixture: A small sample file that tests read as input.
